2.120.m: Kuñjala said: / "Then Nārada saw the divine city named Kāmoda, crowded with all the gods, / for the fulfillment of all desires.
Having reached the home of Kāmodā, the best of the twice-born entered; / and seeing Kāmodā there, filled with all desires,
the brāhmaṇa was honored by her with pleasant words such as greetings. / Seated on a divine seat, the best of the twice-born asked her:
"Are you faring well, fair lady, born of Viṣṇu's splendor?" / And he asked after her good health, greeting her with blessings.
Kāmodā said: / "By the grace of Viṣṇu and yourself, I fare well. / Tell me, O exceedingly wise one, the reason for this question and answer.
A great delusion has arisen in my body, O best of sages, / which pervades all the worlds and destroys the intellect in my body.
From that, sleep arose, just as it occurs among mortals. / And while asleep, O sage, I saw indeed a dreadful dream:
Someone, approaching right before me, said, O best of the twice-born: / 'That unmanifest Hṛṣīkeśa will go into worldly transmigration.'
Since then I have been overcome with sorrow, O high-minded one. / Therefore tell me the cause of that; you are the best among the wise."
Nārada said: / "A dream arising from wind, from bile, from phlegm, or from their combination, / occurs among human beings, fair lady; there is no doubt.
Neither dream nor sleep is born among the gods, O beautiful woman. / A dream seen at the time of sunrise is the highest.
Indeed, a good dream yields the fruit of human beings' merit. / I shall tell you another cause of a dream, O auspicious lady.
Through the shaking of great winds, the waters move, O lovely-faced one; / subtle drops of water break off from that body of water.
Those pure water drops fall outside, O auspicious lady; / again they dissolve, and indeed become visible and invisible.
Listen, O radiant lady, as the manifestation of a dream is told in like manner: / the Ātman is pure, detached, and free from passion and hatred.
Transfixed amidst those constituted of the five gross elements, it remains completely motionless; / and it shines resplendent in the midst of the twenty-six principles.
The pure Ātman is solitary and eternal; having come into contact with Prakṛti, / it moves from its place through its states in the form of wind, when,
from the splendor of the Ātman, a counter-splendor is born. / The auspicious name of that very [counter-splendor] is declared to be the Antarātman.
Just as drops of water become separate from milk, O auspicious lady, / so from the splendor of the Ātman, the Antarātman is declared [to arise].
He is indeed the earth, he is the wind, and he is the space; / he is the water, and he shines [as fire]; these five were made in the beginning.
Born from the splendor of the great Ātman, bearing an impure form, / having attained contact with him, they indeed attain unity.
Through the fault of its own nature, they destroy [it], O fair-faced one; / they desire another body again and again, O lovely-faced one.
This play and diversion of theirs is the cause of association with creation. / A wave of water arises and dissolves;
for such a one, again and again, there is rebirth and loss. / The example is of the form of water, and just so is it with these without doubt.
The Ātman does not perish, O goddess; splendor and wind do not perish; / earth and space do not perish, nor do the waters perish.
Only the five arise and pass away together with the Ātman; / for these, beginning with the Ātman, are eternal in nature, fair lady; there is no doubt.
Only the body perishes, and having been produced for them, / it is destroyed by the severe faults of sense objects, such as passion and hatred.
The vital breaths, comprised of the five [elements], depart from the body, O twice-born one; / at the end of the body dwells the Ātman, and the reflection of it,
the Antarātman, shines just as a spark of fire shines; / thus it comes to light, becoming visible and invisible.
The pure Ātman is the supreme Brahman; it always wakes perpetually; / but the Antarātman is bound by the great qualities of Prakṛti.
Nourished by the intake of food, the Antarātman experiences pleasure; / from extreme pleasure delusion is born, and from that the mind is bewildered.
Afterward, sleep is born, dark and increasing dissolution. / When the sun passes over Mount Meru along the path of channels,
then night occurs until the sun rises; / freed from the darkness of sense objects, the Antarātman shines.
The Antarātman is seized by the states of those constituted of the elements, nourished by the five elements, / through the bodies residing in previous births.
It will indeed go to higher and lower stations, O highly wise one; / in transmigration, the Antarātman, bound by faults, is led along.
The Jīvātman protects the body, standing in the middle afterwards. / The Udāna breath stirs violently; from that, sound is produced.
Just as a dry bellows filled with air produces a breath, / so by the power of sound, the Udāna breath forcibly produces breath.
By the power of the Ātman, the Udāna becomes strong; / thus the body becomes senseless, appearing as if dead.
Then sleep, the great illusion, proceeds into his limbs; / it settles in the heart, in the throat, in the mouth, and at the tip of the nose.
It rests having drawn in the two arms, residing in the heart and in the circle of the navel; / and by the power of the Ātman, the wind named Udāna
becomes extremely violent, and it obstructs the bodily strength. / Just as one bound with a rope is held by a wooden stake,
so too the vital breath is closely attached to the Ātman, there is no doubt; / and the vital breath is attached to the Antarātman, O fair-faced one.
Riding like the intellect, fair lady, the Antarātman rushes along; / remembering the impressions accumulated in previous births, it rushes there.
Stationed there, the highly intelligent one sports again at will; / thus the Antarātman sees dreams of various kinds.
It sees [things] excellent and contrary, connected with action; / and it sees mountains that are very difficult of access, both high and low.
Know that very thing to be from wind; now I speak of that which is from phlegm: / it sees water, a river, a pond, and reservoirs of water;
and it sees fire, O goddess, and abundant, excellent gold. / Know that very thing to be from bile; and I also speak of what is yet to happen.
A dream seen at dawn, whether auspicious or inauspicious, / is connected with karma, O woman of beautiful hips, revealing gain or loss.
The state of the dream has thus been explained to you, O lady of excellent complexion; / and that future event, O woman of beautiful hips, will indeed happen to Viṣṇu.
For that reason, a bad dream was seen by you; indeed, it was observed."

2.121.m: Kāmodā said: / "None of the deities know his end or his form, / in whom all this is dissolved, and who is declared to be the one Ātman;
whose illusion is this cosmic expanse, this transmigration—listen, O Nārada: / why does my lord, the master of the universe, enter transmigration?
A man is bound by actions, by sins and even by good merits, / and wanders in transmigration, O brāhmaṇa; why should Hari go? Tell me."
Nārada said: / "Listen, O goddess; I will explain what was done by that wielder of the discus. / In the presence of Bhṛgu, he made a vow: 'I will protect the sacrifice.'
At the command of Indra, Govinda immediately went to fight / along with the Dānavas, abandoning Bhṛgu's excellent sacrifice.

When the god departed, abandoning the sacrifice, those foremost Dānavas,
evil-minded, came afterwards and destroyed the entire sacrifice.

Enraged, that lord of yogins, Bhṛgu himself, cursed Hari:
“Endure ten births, sullied by my curse!

Janārdana shall experience the fruition of his own karma.
It is for that reason, O goddess, that an evil dream was seen by you.”
Having spoken thus to her, that brāhmaṇa Nārada went to the world of Brahmā; / then she became deeply grieved by the great grief of Kṛṣṇa.

The young woman wept piteously, crying out again and again, “Alas, alas!”
Seated on the bank of the Gaṅgā by the edge of the water, listen, my son:

From her fair eyes she shed tears in her sorrow;
those tears shed by her fell into the water of the Gaṅgā.

And her teardrops sank into the water;
they then arose, dear child, in the form of lotuses.

Blooming in the water of the Gaṅgā, they drifted along;
and the foremost Dānava, deluded by Viṣṇu's māyā, saw them.

He did not know they were born of sorrow, even though recounted by the sage;
overcome with great joy, the Asura seized them.

With those blossoming lotuses he worshiped the beloved of the mountain’s daughter—
with seventy million [lotuses], that lord of Daityas, deluded by Viṣṇu's māyā.

Then the enraged sustainer of the world spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
“Behold the unlawful conduct of this Dānava, O highly intelligent one!

These lotuses born of sorrow that entered the water of the Gaṅgā—
this one gathers them, his mind agitated by desire.

And the evil-minded one worships with things that cause sorrow and torment!
How could supreme welfare come from these flowers born of suffering and grief?

With whatever inner disposition he may worship me,
with such a disposition his attainment shall be.

Devoid of true meditation, his mind fixed on Kāmodā,
he has become wicked in conduct. Slay him, O goddess, with your own splendor!”

Hearing this speech of the great-souled Śambhu, [she said:]
“By your command, O Śambhu, I will bring about his destruction.”

Having spoken thus, the goddess then, desiring his destruction,
was eager; indeed, she pondered a means to slay Vihuṇḍa.

Assuming an illusory form of a noble Brahmin,
she worshiped the lord Śaṅkara with excellent pārijāta flowers.

Approaching, the sinful Dānava destroyed that divine worship;
agitated by desire, afflicted with deep suffering, his mind was directed to her, intent upon her.

The sinful Dānava recalled that great māyā of Viṣṇu
seen before, afflicted as he was by the arrows of desire.

Merely by remembering her, through powerful Kāmadeva,
he, afflicted with suffering and agitated by separation, wept again and again.

Drawn on by death, that wicked-minded one took those [lotuses]
born of sorrow and came desiring to worship Maheśvara.

Destroying out of intense greed the worship performed by the goddess
with excellent pārijāta flowers, he worshiped with those born of grief.

Drops of tears flowing incessantly from the eyes
of that wicked one, dear child, fell upon the top of the liṅga.

The goddess in the form of a Brahmin said to him, “O highly intelligent one,
who are you, constantly worshiping the god with a mind agitated by sorrow?

Tears born of your grief, which are impure, fall upon the head of the god.
Explain this matter before me.”

Vihuṇḍa said:
“Formerly a woman was seen by me, endowed with all good fortune and prosperity,
possessed of all auspicious marks, a great abode of love.

Tormented by infatuation for her, I became overwhelmed with desire.
By her it was said: ‘In our union, grant me an excellent gift:

Worship Maheśvara with flowers born of Kāmodā;
cast a garland made of those flowers upon my neck.

Worship Maheśvara with seventy million [flowers].’
For that purpose I worship the fruit-granting lord

with flowers born of Kāmodā, difficult to obtain even for gods and Dānavas.”
The auspicious goddess said:
“Where is your devotion, where is your meditation, where is your knowledge, O vile-souled one?

There is no connection whatsoever between you and the Lord.
What is the wondrous form of Kāmodā like? Tell me now.

Where were those excellent flowers born from her laughter obtained?”
Vihuṇḍa said:
“I do not know devotion or meditation; she was never seen by me.

I simply take daily those that have entered the water of the Gaṅgā;
with them I worship the sole Śaṅkara, I declare.

It was told to me, O Brahmin, by the noble Śukra;
at his word I worship the lord of the gods day after day.

All this has been told to you, as I was asked just now.”
The auspicious goddess said:
“With those flowers born of sorrow, produced from Kāmodā's weeping,

you worship the liṅga, O wicked one, constantly in the morning.
In whatever disposition and with whatever flowers

the lord of the gods was worshiped by you, obtain a corresponding fruit!
Having thus destroyed the divine worship, you worship with flowers of sorrow.

This very severe fault has arisen in you today;
therefore I will inflict punishment. Suffer the fruit born of your own deed!”

Hearing her words, he, drawn on by death, said:
“Ha, you wicked, ill-behaved fellow, slanderer of my ritual!

I will kill you here with this very sword, of this there is no doubt!”
Having spoken thus to that Brahmin, he drew a sharp sword.

Wishing to kill, that wicked-minded Dānava rushed forward.
That goddess, the supreme ruler in the form of a Brahmin, was greatly enraged.

motionless, shapeshifting, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When that Dānava, the destroyer of all worlds, fell,

all the worlds returned to ease, freed from sorrow and distress.
For this reason, dear child, that woman indeed laments

on the bank of the Gaṅgā, the fair-hipped woman, her mind agitated by grief.
All this has been told to you, which was inquired by you.

Viṣṇu said:
Having spoken thus to his noble son, Kuñjala, the king of birds,
highly wise, ceased, and said nothing further, O king.

2.122.m:
Viṣṇu said:
Having spoken thus to his sons, that Kuñjala, the bird of dharma,
highly wise, fell silent and said nothing more to them.

A foremost twice-born seated beneath a banyan tree said to that great parrot:
“Who are you, an exponent of dharma, existing in the form of a bird?

Are you a god, or a Gandharva, or a Vidyādhara?
By whose curse have you attained this sinful womb of a parrot?

From what cause does such supersensory knowledge exist in you, O parrot?
Is it of some great merit, or the fruit of someone's asceticism?

Or is it in this disguised form, O high-minded one?
Who are you—are you an accomplished adept or a god? Tell me the reason for that.”

Kuñjala said:
“O accomplished one, I know you, your family and your excellent lineage,
your learning and the power of your asceticism, on account of which you roam the earth.
I will tell you everything, O brahmin. Welcome to you, O man of virtuous vows! / Sitting upon an auspicious seat, resort to the cool shade.
Brahmā has the unmanifest as his source; from him was born the Prajāpati. / A brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues was Bhṛgu, a twice-born equal to Brahmā.
His [son] was named Bhārgava, who knew the truth of all dharma and aims of life. / In his lineage, O brahmin, you were born, Cyavana, renowned on earth.
I am neither a god nor a gandharva, nor again am I a vidyādhara. / Who I am, O brahmin, I will tell you; listen to that as I speak.
In Kaśyapa's lineage was born an excellent brāhmaṇa, / who knew the true meaning of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, illuminating all religious duties,
renowned as Vidyādhara, endowed with lineage, good conduct, and virtues, / resplendent at that time with fortune, O brahmin, through his righteous conduct and penance.
Three sons were born to him, that Vidyādhara: / Vasuśarman, Nāmaśarman, and Dharmaśarman were those three.
Among them, I am Dharmaśarman, the youngest, devoid of virtues. / Vasuśarman was my brother, skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and treatises,
richly endowed with conduct and again with excellent qualities such as learning. / Nāmaśarman was very wise, and likewise superior in virtues.
I alone was born a great fool; listen, O best of men! / When [did I ever grasp] the noble meaning, the auspicious import of learning, O brahmin?
I did not listen, nor indeed did I go to the guru's supreme house. / Therefore my father would reflect concerning me thus:
"The name 'Dharmaśarman' for this son is entirely meaningless. / He was born in the world, yet is not learned, nor a mine of virtues for me."
Thinking thus, the righteous-minded one, deeply distressed, said to me: / 'Go, son, to the teacher's house; acquire knowledge.'
Hearing that auspicious statement of my father, [I said]: / "I will not go, father, to the guru's house, which causes great sorrow,
where there is always beating, frowning, shouting, / and where, listen, O best of men, no food is seen by any effort!
Day and night there is no sleep, nor is there any means of comfort. / Therefore, father, I will not go to the guru's dwelling, which is full of misery.
I will not pursue the task of learning; I am eager for play. / By your grace, father, I will eat, sleep, and play,
along with the children, happily, day and night, without laziness." / Knowing me to be a fool, that righteous-souled man, deeply distressed, said to me:
Vidyādhara said: / "Do not act rashly, my son; make an effort for learning! / By learning, comfort, fame, and matchless renown are obtained;
knowledge, heaven, and liberation [are obtained]; therefore accomplish learning. / Though at first having its root in great misery, learning later bestows happiness.
Therefore, my son, master learning! Go to the guru's house!" / Failing to obey my father's command thus day by day,
wherever I stayed, I constantly brought about loss of wealth. / Laughter was made by people, and reviling of me, O brahmin.
Then shame arose in me, destroying my desire for life. / [I thought:] "Endeavouring for learning, O brahmin, to which guru shall I appeal?"
Thus I became overwhelmed with worry, overcome with sorrow and grief: / 'How shall I know learning? How shall I gain virtues?'
How will heaven be mine? How shall I attain liberation?" / Thinking thus, O brahmin, I eventually reached old age.
Once, while I was seated sorrowfully in a temple, / impelled by my fortunes, a certain siddha arrived,
homeless, of controlled diet, ever blissful, and desireless, / dwelling in solitude, O brahmin, engaged in yoga, with conquered senses,
absorbed in the supreme brahman, possessing knowledge, meditation, and concentration. / I resorted to him, O brahmin, the great-minded one who was knowledge embodied.
With a pure disposition, bowing my neck with devotion, / having bowed to that great soul, I stood before him.
Indeed, I was wretched and likewise unfortunate. / By him I was asked, O brahmin: "Why do you grieve deeply?
With what intention or state of mind do you experience only sorrow?" / Thus was I addressed then, O prince of brahmins, by that wise yogin.
By me, thoroughly foolish, my past history was indeed related / all to him, [saying]: "How might one attain omniscience?
For this purpose I am in great misery; you are ever my refuge!" / And that great soul explained to me all the causes of knowledge.

2.123.m: The siddha said: / "Listen! I will explain the nature of knowledge before you. / Knowledge indeed has no body, no hands, feet, or eyes.
Knowledge has neither nose nor ears, nor indeed any collection of bones. / By whom then has knowledge been seen, and what are its marks?
It is eternally devoid of forms; it knows everything, omniscient. / The sun is the illuminator by day, and the moon illuminates by night;
a lamp illuminates a house; these exist within the world. / By what splendour then is that abode seen? Listen, O best of men!
Those fools do not find it, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu. / Knowledge resides within the body, radiant through meditation, incomparable.
That abode may be seen by it, and not by the moon, sun, or other [luminaries]. / Knowledge is without hands and feet, devoid of eyes and ears;
its movement is everywhere; it grasps all and sees all; / it smells everything, O prince of brahmins, and hears: of this there is no doubt.
There is no lamp equal to knowledge in destroying all darkness. / In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, it is seen in place after place.
Those of evil intellect do not find knowledge situated within the body. / I shall tell you the seat of knowledge, from which knowledge is born.
It is eternally placed in the hearts of living beings at all times, O twice-born. / Whoever desires always to burn up with the fire of discernment
the very great objects of enjoyment, such as desire, as well as great delusion and the rest, / having become completely full of tranquility, should crush the objects of the senses.
From that arises knowledge, revealing the meaning of all principles of reality. / This knowledge, pure and seeing everything, is rooted in reality.
Therefore, cultivate peace, which fosters all happiness: / equal toward enemy and friend, as toward oneself so toward another.
Be always self-restrained, of subdued diet, with senses conquered. / Friendship should not be cultivated, and enmity should be cast far away.
Free from attachment, desireless, taking refuge in a solitary place, / you will become an all-illuminating knower, seeing all.
Standing in a single place, my child, whatever event shall occur / in the three worlds, you will know by my grace; there is no doubt."
Kuñjala said: / "O brahmin, by that siddha the nature of knowledge was illuminated for me. / Always standing by his word, imbued with his very disposition,
whatever exists in the three worlds, even while staying in a single place, / all that I know by the grace of that good guru.
All this has been recounted to you, namely, my own history. / What else shall I tell you? Say that, O best of twice-born!"

Cyavana said:
How did you, the best of the wise, obtain the birth of a parrot? / Tell me the cause of that, which will destroy all my doubt.

Kuñjala said:
Evil arises from association; from association alone arises merit. / Therefore a pure person should abandon what is harmful and contradictory [to virtue].
By a certain sinful hunter, a single young parrot / was brought bound, intent on selling it.
Seeing that charming, handsome bird with clever speech, / he was bought by a brāhmaṇa and given to me with affection.
Constantly absorbed in knowledge and meditation though I was, O best of the twice-born, / by his childlike nature, he stayed in my hand out of playful curiosity.
Bewitched by his playful words, O best of the twice-born, / my mind was ever intent upon that parrot who was like a son.
He would speak to me thus: “Father, father, sit down! / Go bathe, fortunate one! Worship the deity now!”
She would speak to me with such flattering words and the like; / through the diversion of her talk, that supreme knowledge was forgotten.
When I had gone into the forest for flowers and fruit to eat, / the parrot was carried off by a cat, to the cause of my grief.
By all my companions, virtuous companions who associated with me, [it was said]: / “The bird was killed by a cat, and was indeed devoured by it.”
Hearing, O brāhmaṇa, that that sweet-speaking parrot had met death, / I was deeply afflicted by intense grief, in misery.
Bewildered by grief for him, severely pained indeed, / I was bound by a great snare of delusion, O bull among the twice-born.
My mind agitated by delusion, I lamented, O brāhmaṇa: / “O Rāmabhadra! O king of parrots! O learned one! O king of verses!”
Then, tormented by sorrow brought about by my own deed / through separation from the parrot, listen now, O chief of the twice-born!
That knowledge revealed by the Siddha was forgotten by me, / tormented by sorrow as I continually remembered that sweet-speaking parrot.
Constantly lamenting, “Child, child!”, listen, O descendant of Bhṛgu, / in words consisting of prose and verse, endowed with cultured syllables:
“Without you, child, who will now instruct me, / pleasing me with wonderful stories, O king of birds?
Where have you gone, leaving me in this completely lonely garden? / By what fault have I been tainted? Tell me that now!”
Bewildered by such plaintive words as these, / lamenting in such ways, and severely afflicted by sorrow,
I died from that delusion, also bewitched by that disposition. / Whatever disposition and whatever thought one has at death,
with just such a disposition was I born, O best of the twice-born. / Dwelling in the womb was experienced by me, which produces memory of knowledge.
Past actions performed by my own effort were remembered: / “What has been done by me, a sinful, foolish, uncontrolled soul?”
Engaged in contemplation in the womb, I meditated upon him again. / By that, pure knowledge arose in me, revealing all.
And by the grace of that guru, supreme knowledge was attained; / by the pure water of his words, the impurity of the body
was washed away inside and out, O brāhmaṇa, and made clean. / Yet I attained an animal state, born of the parrot species,
due to the state of meditating on the parrot when death arrived. / At that time I died, O brāhmaṇa, thoroughly imbued with that state.
As such, I was born again on the earth in the form of a parrot. / Whatever disposition arises in living beings at the moment of death,
such those beings become: possessing that form, devoted to that, / having those qualities, bearing that essential nature, becoming creatures of that disposition.
Through the state of mind at the time of death, O chief of the twice-born, there is no doubt. / Here I have attained incomparable knowledge, O high-minded one.
By it I see everything that was, that will be, / and that is present, O highly wise, high-minded one, through this knowledge.
I know everything, even staying right here, without any doubt. / For the crossing over of human beings turning in the cycle of transmigration,
there is no sacred ford equal to the guru, which cuts bonds, O twice-born. / All this has been told to you; listen, O delight of the Bhṛgus!
Whatever was asked by you, O brāhmaṇa, all that has been explained to you. / By water born of the earth, all external impurity is destroyed;
the guru-ford destroys sins committed in other lives. / The mobile sacred ford is supreme for delivering one from worldly existence.

Viṣṇu said:
Having thus revealed the truth to the great-souled Cyavana, O highly wise one, / the parrot paused, O best of kings.
All this has been told to you: the supreme, mobile sacred ford. / Choose a boon—blessing unto you!—whatever is in your mind.

Vena said:
I have no desire for kingship, nor do I desire anything else. / I wish to go bodily into your form, O Janārdana.

This is the boon I ask, if you wish to grant one here.
Viṣṇu said:
Sacrifice with the horse sacrifice and the Rājasūya, O ruler of the earth!
Make gifts of cows, land, gold, water, and grains, O high-minded one! / Through giving, indeed, terrible sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa are destroyed.
The four aims of life are certainly accomplished through giving, there is no doubt. / Therefore, giving must be performed dedicated to me, O king.
With whatever disposition one gives, dedicating it to me, / such a state do I truly make for him.
From the sight and touch of the sages, your accumulation of sins has fallen away. / At the end of the sacrifice you shall enter my body, there is no doubt.
Having thus spoken to Vena, Hari disappeared.

2.124.m:
Thus ends the hundred and twenty-third chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the narrative of Vena, in the description of the completion of the glorification of the Guru as a sacred place, and the conclusion of the story of Cyavana.

Devoted to all virtues, they engaged in gifts and enjoyments; / they flourished with all happiness through the grace of that king.

Thus ends the one hundred twenty-fourth chapter, the episode of Vena, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

The hundred and twenty-fifth chapter. / Sūta said: Having received Vena's command, Pṛthu, the most righteous, / the king's son, collected all materials of various holy kinds.

Having invited all the brahmins, even those born in diverse regions, / that king then performed the horse sacrifice for Vena.

He gave gifts of various kinds, in abundance, to the brahmins; / the lord of the earth went to the realm of Viṣṇu in his own body.

Together with Viṣṇu that righteous one abides forever. / Thus the entire deed of that king has been related to you,

which calms all sins and destroys all sorrows. / That righteous king Pṛthu ruled this earth;

the best of kings milked this earth together with the three worlds, / and the subjects were delighted by him through virtuous and righteous deeds.

All this unsurpassed Bhūmikhaṇḍa has been told to you: / the first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and the second is the Bhūmikhaṇḍa.

2.124.m:
I shall tell again the glorification of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa: / whatever best of men hears a single verse of this section,

the sin of a single day of his is destroyed. / The wise man who, endowed with devotion, listens to a chapter,

I will tell his merit; hear it, O best of the twice-born: / the fruit that would arise from giving a thousand cows to brahmins on an auspicious day,

that fruit arises, and Viṣṇu is pleased with him. / For one constantly reciting this Padma Purāṇa,

in the Kali age no obstacles arise for a man at all." / Vyāsa said: "Why do no obstacles arise in the Kali age for one who listens, O lotus-born one,

even though for a man endowed with merit, various terrible obstacles occur?" / Brahmā said: "Whatever fruit is proclaimed of the horse sacrifice,

that fruit is seen, my dear, in the Purāṇa named the Padma. / The sacred horse sacrifice does not take place in the Kali age;

and the Purāṇa is celebrated as equal to that horse sacrifice. / The merit of the horse sacrifice bestows the fruit of heaven and liberation;

sinful men, established on the paths of sin, do not enjoy it. / Men do not enjoy the merit equal to the horse sacrifice
