2.124.m: with great Vaiṣṇava mantras, with Viṣṇu hymns granting supreme merit, / with the 'Viṣṇoḥ Rarāṭam' mantra, and with the thousand-headed hymn;
with the auspicious mantra 'Idaṃ Viṣṇuḥ', with the 'Ābrahman' mantra repeatedly, / and with the 'Tryambaka' mantra, he should thus perform the fire offering;
with the excellent Bṛhatsāman mantra, and with the twelve-syllable mantra; / for whatever deity the offering is intended, with the mantra of that deity he should offer;
with one hundred and eight offerings of sesame, clarified butter, and Palāśa firewood; / the installation and worship of the planets also must be done, O twice-born one.
There he should worship the Lord of Obstacles, and Śāradā, the ruler of the gods, / Jātavedas, Mahāmāyā, Caṇḍikā, and the guardian of the sacred ground;
with sesamum, grains of rice, and clarified butter, accompanied by their mantras, / thus the fire offering should be performed, and he should give wealth to the brahmins.
He should give a sacrificial fee according to his capacity, accompanied by a cow, my child; / then the obstacles perish, and the Purāṇa attains fulfillment.
For him who indeed does not do this, I will describe the obstacle: / in his body a disease is born that causes great distress;
sorrow over a wife, sorrow over a son, and loss of wealth arise; / he suffers various major diseases—there is no doubt of this.
He in whose house there is no wealth should observe a fast; / having reached the eleventh day, he should worship Madhusūdana
with the sixteen offerings and with a mind endowed with devotion; / afterwards he should feed the brahmins according to his means.
Then, having given the resolved offering endowed with oblation to Keśava, / the wise man should himself take food together with his relatives,
joined by his sons and wife; then he will attain fulfillment. / The complete Purāṇa compilation should be heard by those intent on righteousness.

The attainment of the four aims of life comes to him indeed, not otherwise.
Hear the one hundred and twenty-five thousand [verses] named Brahmā, belonging to Puṣkara,

which sinless men hear in the Kṛta age, O twice-born.
Then, the whole Purāṇa named Padma, half of a hundred thousand,

surpassed by two thousand verses,
when men hear it when the Tretā age has arrived,

having enjoyed the fruit of the four aims of life, they will go again to Hari.
Twenty-two thousand is the collection called Padma,

which was spoken in Dvāpara, O priest, by Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
That collection named Padma is only twelve thousand [verses]

which men devoted to Viṣṇu will read in the Kali age.
A single purpose and a single import are set forth across all four

collections, O best of priests, an extensive recounting by Śeṣa.
Only twelve thousand will avoid destruction, O best of beings,

when the Kali age has arrived; it will be the first.
Hearing the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, a person is freed from all sins;

he is freed from all sorrows, he is freed from all diseases.
Abandoning everything else—recitation, charity, and tradition—

one should hear with effort this sin-destroying [Purāṇa] called Padma.
The first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and the second is the Bhūmikhaṇḍa;

the third is the Svargakhaṇḍa, and the fourth is the Pātāla;
and the fifth is the Uttarakhaṇḍa, destroying all sins.

The person who hears the five sections in sequence with devotion,
that mortal obtains the fruit of a thousand gifts of cattle.

3.0.m:
Now the third [section], the Svargakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa is begun.
— Homage to the Remover of Obstacles. — Homage to the Auspicious One.

3.1.m:
I bow to Govinda’s lotus foot, ever praised by Indirā and rich in excellence,
which rests in the heart of the world’s creatures, the sole refuge of great souls, supreme among the highest.

Once all the sages, resembling blazing fires,
all dwellers in the Himālaya, sages who had crossed to the far shore of the Vedas,

knowers of the three times, great-souled, resorting to various meritorious deeds,
those devoted to Mount Mahendra and those dwelling in the Vindhyas,

those engaged in the Arbuda forest, dwellers in the Puṣkara forest,
those devoted to Śrīśaila and dwellers in Kurukṣetra,

those devoted to Dharmāraṇya and dwellers in the Daṇḍaka forest,
those devoted to Jambūmārga and dwellers in Satya[loka],

these and many other pure sages with their disciples,
eager to see Śaunaka, arrived at Naimiṣa.

Having honoured him according to rule, and well honoured by him,
upon various seats, grass mats and the like in due order,

given by Śaunaka, those whose wealth was asceticism sat,
and then spoke among one another holy tales concerning Kṛṣṇa.

Then, at the close of those tales of the sages whose souls were purified,
there arrived Sūta of great splendour and immense brilliance,

the disciple of Vyāsa, knower of the Purāṇas, named Romaharṣaṇa.
Having bowed to them properly, he was also honoured by them.

The great sages, Śaunaka and the others, to Romaharṣaṇa Sūta,
Vyāsa's disciple who had taken his seat comfortably as was fitting,

those blessed ones whose wealth was asceticism, Śaunaka and the others, asked him:
The sages said:
O Sūta of great intellect, faithful to your vows, knower of the Purāṇas,

previously holy tales of ancient times were heard from you;
and now we are ready for a tale of Hari, having leisure.

That is indeed the highest duty of men from which arises devotion to Adhokṣaja;
tell once again a Purāṇa containing the accounts of Hari.

A tale other than Hari's, O Sūta, is held to be like a cremation ground.
Hari stands directly in the form of a holy ford—that has been heard.

Proclaim indeed the names of the sacred places that bestow merit.
From what did this [world] arise, or by whom is it preserved?

Into what does this universe of the moving and unmoving dissolve?
What are the holy fields, and which mountains are to be worshipped?

And what are the supreme, meritorious, auspicious rivers that remove human sins?
O highly fortunate one, tell all this in due order.

Sūta said:
Well said, well said, O fortunate ones! It was well asked, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Having bowed to him, I shall declare the Purāṇa called Padma.

The son of Parāśara, the Supreme Person, the single origin knowable through all things, the vessel of knowledge, bestower of vast intellect, knowable through the Veda and the Vedānta,
always tranquil, the domain of one’s own intellect, vast with pure brilliance,
Vedavyāsa of widespread fame—him I ever revere.

Homage to that blessed Vyāsa of immeasurable splendour,
by whose grace I shall speak this story of Nārāyaṇa.

I shall proclaim the highly meritorious Purāṇa named Padma,
consisting of fifty-five thousand [verses] accompanied by six sections.

There the Ādikhaṇḍa should be first, and after that the Bhūmikhaṇḍa;
then the Brahmakhaṇḍa after that, and then the Pātālakhaṇḍa;

then the celebrated Kriyākhaṇḍa, and the Uttarakhaṇḍa is the last.
This is that very wonderful, great lotus of which the world is made;

because it rests upon that account, it is called Pādma by the wise.
This stainless Purāṇa is the supreme glorification of Viṣṇu,

just as Hari, the God of gods, spoke it of old to Brahmā;
Brahmā told it to Nārada, and Nārada before our guru.

Vyāsa taught all the Purāṇas, together with the legendary histories and collections,
again and again to me, his very dear [pupil].

Therefore I shall declare to you this very rare Purāṇa,
hearing which a mortal is freed from sins such as the slaying of a priest.

And whoever hears it obtains ablution in all sacred places.
Through supreme faith and devotion, merely upon being heard, it grants liberation.

Even if heard without faith, one obtains an accumulation of merit;
therefore make the Padma a guest of your ears with every effort.

First I shall declare the holy Ādikhaṇḍa, which destroys sin.
Let all the sages listen, together with their disciples who are present here.

3.2.m:
Sūta said:
First I shall tell of the primal creation, O best of priests,
by which the eternal Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord, is known.

Among created things, after the dissolution there was nothing, O best of priests;
there was only a single light called Brahman, the maker of all,

eternal, untainted, tranquil, stainless, ever-pure,
an ocean of bliss, transparent, which seekers of liberation desire,

omniscient because its nature is consciousness, infinite, unborn, imperishable,
indestructible, ever clear, unswerving, pervasive, and vast.

When the time of creation arrived, knowing that [light] whose form is knowledge
and its modification merged in the Self, it undertook to create that.

From that arose pradhāna, and from it also the great principle (mahat);
the great principle is threefold: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.

It was indeed enveloped by pradhāna, just as a seed is enveloped by its skin.
Vaikārika, taijasa, and bhūtādi—which is tāmasa—

this threefold ego was born from the principle of mahat.
Just as the great principle was enveloped by pradhāna, so was it enveloped by the great principle.

Bhūtādi, undergoing transformation, produced therefrom the subtle element of sound;
from the subtle element of sound it created space, whose characteristic is sound.

Bhūtādi equally enveloped the subtle element of sound and space;
the subtle element of sound and space then created the subtle element of touch.

From that powerful wind arose; touch is considered to be its quality.
Space, as the subtle element of sound, enveloped the subtle element of touch.

Then the wind, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of form;
from the wind arose light, and form is said to be its quality.

The wind, as the subtle element of touch, enveloped the subtle element of form;
and light, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of taste.

From that arose the waters, which possess the subtle element of taste;
and the waters, possessing the subtle element of taste, enveloped the subtle element of form.

The waters, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of smell;
from that this earth was born, abounding in the qualities of all elements.

Because it is an aggregate, therefore smell is considered its quality.
Because each [quality] is present in its respective [element] as that alone, it is remembered as tanmātra.

The subtle elements are indeterminate; the subsequent ones are gradually determinate.
This creation of the elements and subtle elements is from the tāmasa ego.

It has been proclaimed in brief, O best of sages rich in austerity!
They say that the senses are taijasa, and the ten deities are vaikārika.

The mind is also proclaimed as the eleventh here by the contemplators of reality.
Here are five organs of sense and five organs of action;

I shall proclaim them and their functions, O purifiers of families:
ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose as the fifth;

these are the five endowed with intellect for the purpose of perceiving sound and the rest.
Anus, genitals, hands, feet, and speech is proclaimed as the fifth;

their functions are remembered as excretion, pleasure, grasping, locomotion, and speaking.
Likewise space, wind, fires, water, and earth,

endowed successively with the qualities of sound and the rest, O brāhmaṇas,
possessed various potencies and were separate; therefore, without uniting,

they were unable to produce creatures without coming together completely.
Having formed a mutual combination and relying on each other,

forming a single aggregate and having a common purpose, attaining complete oneness,
because of being presided over by the Spirit and through the favor of pradhāna,

those principles, beginning with the great principle and ending with the determinate elements, produced the egg.
Gradually it grew, constantly resembling a water bubble.

From the elements arose the egg, O highly wise one, and having grown, it lay in the water—
the material, unsurpassed dwelling of Viṣṇu in the form of Brahmā.

There that lord Viṣṇu, master of the universe, whose nature is unmanifest,
having assumed the form of Brahmā, remained of his own accord.

Its amnion was the sweat-born egg, and the mountains were its chorion;
the oceans were the amniotic fluid of that Great Self.

With mountains, continents, and oceans, along with the luminaries—the entire universe,
together with gods, asuras, and humans, came to be within that egg.

The lotus which arose from the navel of Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end,
that became the golden egg by the will of glorious Keśava.

Bearing the quality of rajas, the supreme lord Hari himself,
having assumed the form of Brahmā, sets out to create the universe.

And he protects what was created in each cosmic age as long as the kalpa unfolds;
in the form of Narasiṃha and others, and in the form of Rudra, he dissolves it.

That Great Self, casting off the form of Brahmā, wishing to protect the entire universe,
moves about having taken the form of Rāma and others, and became Rudra to consume this universe.

3.3.m:
The sages said:
[Tell us] the names of the rivers and mountains in their entirety,
as well as of the realms and whatever else rests upon the earth,

and the extent of the earth on all sides, O knower of measures;
explain it fully, along with the forests, O best of beings!

earth, water, wind, fire, and space;
they all increase in qualities [successively], and among them earth is chief.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these qualities of earth have been taught by the sages who know reality.

There are four qualities in water, O brāhmaṇas; smell does not exist there.
Sound, touch, and form are the three qualities of fire.

Sound and touch belong to wind, and only sound is in space.
These five qualities, O brāhmaṇas, abide in the five great elements

in all the worlds in which beings are established;
they do not transgress one another, and then balance prevails.

When, however, they enter into a state of disparity with one another,
then embodied beings come into existence through bodies, not otherwise.

They perish in succession and are born in succession;
they are all immeasurable; that is their divine form.

Wherever they are seen, the five-elemental bodies move about;
humans describe their dimensions through reasoning.

Those realities that are indeed inconceivable one should not establish by reasoning.
I shall describe the island of Sudarśana, O best of sages!

This island is circular, O fortunate ones, situated like a wheel,
intersected by river waters and by mountains resembling the ocean,

with cities of various shapes and delightful realms,
endowed with trees bearing flowers and fruits, prosperous, having wealth and grain,

surrounded entirely on all sides by the salt ocean.
Just as a man would see his own face in a mirror,

so the island Sudarśana is seen as a circular disc:
in two parts of it is a peepal tree, and in two parts is a great hare,

bringing together all herbs, enveloped on all sides;
other waters are to be known beyond it; the rest is told in brief.

The sages said:
That of which a summary was spoken by you according to rule, O intelligent one—
and you know the truth of everything—tell us in detail, O Sūta!

Tell the extent of as much earthly space as is seen in the mark of the hare;
then you will speak of the peepal tree.

Being thus questioned by them, that Sūta then spoke these words:
Sūta said: Extending to the east, O highly wise ones, are these six jewel-mountains,

plunging on both sides into the two oceans, eastern and western:
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha, the excellent mountain,

Nīla made of lapis lazuli, and Śveta resembling the moon,
and the mountain named Śṛṅgavat, studded with all minerals.

These indeed are the mountains, O brāhmaṇas, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas;
the intermediate distances between them are thousands of yojanas.

There lie the holy realms; they are the continents (varṣa), O best of men;
in them dwell beings of diverse kinds on all sides.

This is the realm of Bhārata; beyond it is Haimavata;
and beyond Hemakūṭa they declare Harivarṣa.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha, / extending eastwards, O fortunate ones, lies the mountain named Mālyavān.
Beyond Mālyavān is the mountain Gandhamādana. / Circular between the two is Meru, the golden mountain.
Resembling the morning sun, like a smokeless fire, / it is eighty-four thousand yojanas high.
It [extends] eighty-four [thousand] yojanas below, O best of the twice-born; / it stands encompassing the worlds above, below, and across.
On its sides are situated these four continents, O twice-born ones: / Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and Jambūdvīpa, O best of men,
and the Northern Kurus, the abodes of those of accomplished merit. / The bird named Sumukha, indeed the son of Supārśva,
reflected upon beholding crows turned golden: / 'Meru makes no distinction among highest, middle,
and lowest birds; therefore, I shall abandon it.' / Around it moves the sun, the foremost of luminaries, constantly,
and the moon along with the constellations, and the wind, circumambulating it clockwise. / That mountain, O highly wise ones, is endowed with celestial flowers,
surrounded everywhere by auspicious palaces made of Jambūnada gold. / There hosts of gods, O priests, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas,
joined by troops of Apsarases, constantly sport upon the mountain. / There Brahmā, Rudra, and Śakra, the lord of the gods,
assemble and sacrifice with various offerings accompanied by bountiful sacrificial fees. / Tumburu, Nārada, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū,
approaching the foremost of immortals, praise [them] with varied hymns. / The great-souled Seven Sages and Kaśyapa the Prajāpati
go there—may you have good fortune—always on every sacred lunar day. / On its summit, Uśanas Kāvya is revered by the Daityas.
His are the golden jewels, his are these jewel-mountains; / from that, the blessed Kubera receives a fourth share,
and from that he grants a minute fraction of wealth to humans. / In the interior of the mountain is a divine forest,
a charming grove of Karṇikāra trees filled with flowers of all seasons and raised upon a network of rocks. / There Paśupati in person, surrounded by divine beings,
accompanied by Umā, the blessed originator of beings, delights, / wearing a Karṇikāra garland hanging down to his feet,
giving forth light with his three eyes as if by three risen suns. / Siddhas of severe austerities, of good vows, who speak truth,
behold him, for Maheśvara cannot be seen by the wicked. / From the summit of that mountain, O best of the twice-born,
from the universal form, boundless, with a roar like a dreadful thunderclap, / the sacred and auspicious Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī, frequented by the purest of beings,
flows with great speed into the auspicious lake of the Moon; / by her was that sacred lake, resembling the ocean, created.
Then, difficult to hold even by mountains, the wielder of the Pināka / bore her upon his head for a hundred thousand years.
On the western side of Meru is Ketumāla, O best of the twice-born; / in that very region of Jambū, O twice-born ones, is a great province.
The lifespan there is ten thousand years, O best of men; / the men are of golden complexion, and the women are equal to Apsarases.
Free from disease, devoid of sorrow, their minds ever joyful, / men are born there shining like refined gold.
On the peaks of Gandhamādana, Kubera, together with the Rākṣasas / and surrounded by hosts of Apsarases, rejoices as the lord of the Guhyakas.
On the other side of Gandhamādana are those freed from sins; / their maximum lifespan is eleven thousand years.
There the men are dark, O priests, endowed with radiance, of great strength, / and all the women resemble blue lotus petals, exceedingly lovely to behold.
Holding the blue lotus is the white [realm]; beyond Śveta is the excellent Hiraṇyaka realm; / and the Airāvata realm, O priests, is filled with various provinces.
The two bow-shaped realms, O fortunate ones, are the southern and northern realms; / Ilāvṛta is situated in the middle, and there are five realms.
Successively higher than these, each realm is superior in qualities: / in length of life, health, dharma, desire, and wealth.
All beings in them are endowed [with these], O best of men. / Thus, O fortunate ones, this earth is covered with mountains.
Hemakūṭa is a very great mountain named Kailāsa; / there the god Vaiśravaṇa rejoices together with the Guhyakas.
To the north of Kailāsa, towards Mount Maināka, / is a very great celestial mountain made of jewels, named Hiraṇyaśṛṅga.
At its side is a great, celestial, bright, charming lake named Viṣṇusaras / with golden sands, where King Bhagīratha,
having seen Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī, dwelt for many years. / There the sacrificial posts are made of jewels, and the grounds are golden.
Having sacrificed there, the thousand-eyed one of great fame attained perfection. / Where the eternal Creator, the Lord of prosperity, by all the worlds
is worshipped, of fierce radiance, where the Being is present on all sides: / Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Manu, and Sthāṇu as the fifth.
There the celestial river of three paths was first established; / departing from the world of Brahmā, she proceeds sevenfold:
Vaṭodakā, Nalinī, Pārvatī, and Sarasvatī, / the river Jambū, Sītā, and the seventh, Gaṅgā-Sindhu.
Inconceivable, known as celestial, she is endowed with powers; / where a sacrificial session is celebrated at the turn of a thousand yugas,
there Sarasvatī becomes visible and invisible here and there. / These are the seven celestial Gaṅgās renowned throughout the three worlds.
The Rākṣasas dwell on Himavān, and the Guhyakas on Hemakūṭa; / serpents and nāgas on Niṣadha, and the penance grove Gokarṇa.
Mount Śveta is said to belong to all the gods and Asuras; / Gandharvas ever reside on Niṣadha, and likewise Brahmanical sages on Nīla.
Śṛṅgavān, O fortunate ones, is the resort of the gods. / Thus, O fortunate ones, are these seven realms divided into parts.
Beings are settled in them, both mobile and immobile; / their prosperity is seen to be manifold, both divine and human.
It is impossible to enumerate, but it should be trusted as adorned. / As to that celestial hare-shaped form about which you asked me, O priests:
the two realms on the flanks of the hare are stated to be the southern and northern ones; / on the ear are Nāgadvīpa and Kāśyapadvīpa,

and the jewel of Karṇadvīpa, O priests, is the glorious mountain Malaya. / This is seen as the second [form] of the continent, resembling a hare.

Thus ends the third chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious and great Padma Purāṇa.

3.4.m: The sages said: / Next tell us, Sūta, about the north, west, and east of Meru, / and fully, O greatly wise one, about Mount Mālyavān.
Sūta said: / To the south of Nīla, and likewise on the northern side of Meru, / are the Northern Kurus, O priests, sacred and inhabited by Siddhas.
There the trees bear honey-fruits, constantly yielding flowers and fruits; / the flowers are fragrant and the fruits full of delicious juice.
There some trees yield all desires for livelihood, O best of the twice-born; / there are other trees there named milky trees, O best of the twice-born,
which always pour forth milk resembling nectar, all of them; / and garments and ornaments are produced among their fruits.
The entire ground is made of jewels, with fine golden sand, / pleasant to the touch in all seasons, and fruitless, O rich in asceticism.
All the men are born there having fallen from the world of the gods, / endowed with noble, pure ancestry, all very pleasing to behold.
Twins, both male and female, are born, and the women resemble apsarases; / they drink the milk of those milk-bearing trees, which is like nectar.
A pair is born together, and together they grow up, / endowed with equal beauty and virtues, and similarly with equal dress,
matched to one another alone, resembling cakravāka birds, O twice-born ones; / and those people are free from disease, their minds ever joyful.
They live for ten thousand years / and ten hundred years, those fortunate ones, nor do they ever leave one another.
Birds named bhāruṇḍas, sharp-beaked and of great strength, / carry away the dead here and throw them into caves.
The northern Kurus have been explained to you in brief, O brahmins; / I shall now declare as it truly is the eastern side of Meru.
The crowning crest of Bhadrāśva, O rich in asceticism, / is where the Bhadraśāla forest is, and the great trees called kālāmras.
The kālāmras, O fortunate ones, are auspicious, ever with flowers and fruits; / the trees are a yojana in height, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.
There the men are white, endowed with luster and great strength; / and the women have the complexion of white water-lilies, beautiful and pleasing to behold,
having the hue of the moon, belonging to the four castes, their faces like the full moon, / their limbs cool as the moon, and skilled in dance and song.
The lifespan there is ten thousand years, O best of the twice-born; / having drunk the juice of the kālāmra fruit, they are established in perpetual youth.
To the south of Nīla, but to the north of Niṣadha, / is a great eternal jambū tree named Sudarśana.
It yields the fruit of all desires, is sacred, and is frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas; / by its name the eternal Jambūdvīpa is proclaimed.
One thousand and one hundred yojanas [in extent], O best of the twice-born, / similarly on the eastern peak of Mālyavat, ending in the eastern regions,
Mālyavat is fifty thousand yojanas [in extent], O twice-born ones; / men are born there resembling great silver.
All have fallen from the world of Brahmā, and all are expounders of the Veda; / they perform divine asceticism and are indeed chaste in seed.
For the protection of living beings they enter the sun; / sixty thousand and sixty hundred of them
go before Aruṇa, encircling the sun / for sixty thousand years and sixty hundred [years];

scorched by the heat of the sun, they enter the orb of the moon.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious and great Padma Purāṇa.

3.5.m: The sages said: / O most virtuous one, tell us truly the names of the realms and of the mountains, / as well as those who dwell upon the mountains.
Sūta said: / To the south of Śveta, but to the north of Niṣadha, / is the realm named Ramaṇaka; men are born there
endowed with noble, pure ancestry, all of them pleasing to behold; / and all those men are born free from rivals.
They live for ten thousand years / and fifteen hundred [years], those fortunate ones, their minds ever joyful.
To the south of Nīla, but to the north of Niṣadha, / is the realm named Hiraṇmaya, where flows the river Haimavatī,
and where is that king of birds, the best of winged creatures, O highly wise ones; / [men there] follow the sacrifice, are excellent brahmins, archers, and pleasing to behold;
the people there are of great strength, O brahmins, with joyful minds; / their lifespan is eleven thousand years,
and fifteen hundred [years] they live, O rich in asceticism. / And there are three sacred peaks, O best among the twice-born:
one there is made of jewels, similarly one is wondrous gold, / and one is made of all kinds of gems, adorned with mansions.
There the self-luminous goddess Śaṇḍinī resides perpetually. / To the north of Śṛṅga, bordering the ocean, O best of the twice-born,
is the realm named Airāvata, beyond that Śṛṅgavat; / there the sun has no course, nor do men grow old;
and the moon, together with the asterisms, is encompassed like a luminary. / Men are born there having the luster of a lotus, the hue of a lotus, eyes like lotus petals,
and with the sweet fragrance of lotus petals; / they are complete, free of foul odor, without food, and with conquered senses,
all fallen from the world of the gods, and free from passion, O twice-born ones; / their lifespan is thirteen thousand years,
and they live that measure, those men who are preeminent in righteousness, O best of the twice-born. / Likewise, to the north of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord
Hari, Vaikuṇṭha, stands upon a golden chariot; / that vehicle has eight wheels, is attended by spirits, and is swift as thought,
fire-colored, of great splendor, and adorned with refined gold. / He is the Lord of all beings and the all-pervading ruler, O best of the twice-born,
both in brief and in detail, the creator and the cause of action, / the earth, water, space, wind, and fire, O best of men;

He is the sacrifice of all creatures; the fire that eats offerings is his mouth.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.

3.6.m: The sages said: / Tell us all about this auspicious realm of Bhārata that produces merit, / for we consider you to be wise.
Sūta said: / Here I shall proclaim to you the supreme realm of Bhārata, / dear to the god Mitra and to Vaivasvata Manu,
and to the wise Pṛthu, the son of Vena, and likewise to the high-souled Ikṣvāku, / to Yayāti, Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, and Nahuṣa,
and also to Mucukunda, Kubera, Uśīnara, / to Ṛṣabha, Ila, and king Nṛga,
and to Kuśika the royal sage, and the high-souled Gādhi, / and to the royal sage Soma, and likewise to Dilīpa,
and to other powerful, highly fortunate kṣatriyas; / supreme Bhārata is dear indeed to all living beings.
Therefore I shall describe this realm to you as I have heard it, O great twice-born ones: / Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, Ṛkṣavān,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra: these seven are the principal mountain ranges. / Near them, O brāhmaṇas, are thousands of mountains,
unrecognized, substantial, vast, and having marvelous peaks; / and others that are well-known, small, sustaining short [peoples].
These men, sharing the customs of Āryas and Mlecchas, mixed together, O twice-born ones, / drink from the clear river Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sarasvatī,
the Godāvarī, the Narmadā, and the great river Bahudā, / the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the great river Yamunā,
the Dṛṣadvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāpā of pure sand, / the river Vetravatī, the Kṛṣṇā, and the river Veṇī,
the Irāvatī, the Vitastā, the Payoṣṇī, the Devikā, / the Vedasmṛti, the Vedaśiras, the Tridivā, the Sindhuvikṛmi,
the Karīṣiṇī, the Citravahā, and the river Trisenā, / the Gomatī, the Dhūtapāpā, and the great river Candanā,
the Kauśikī, the Tridivā, the charming Nācitā, the Rohitāraṇī, / the Rahasyā, the Śatakumbhā, and the Sarayū, O best of the twice-born,
the Carmaṇvatī, the Vetravatī, the Hastisomā, the Diś, / the Śarāvatī, the Payoṣṇī, the Bhīmā, and the Bhīmarathī,
the Kāverī, the Culukā, the Tāpī, the Śatamalā, / the Nīvārā, the Mahitā, and the river Suprayogā,
the Pavitrā, the Kṛṣṇalā, the Sindhu, the Vājinī, the Puramālinī, / the Pūrvābhirāmā, the Vīrā, the Bhīmā, and the Mālāvatī,
the Palāśinī, the Pāpaharā, the Mahendrā, the Paṭalāvatī, / the Karīṣiṇī, the Asiknī, and the great river Kuśacīrī,
the Marudvṛdhā, the Pravarā, the Menā, the Hemā, and the Ghṛtavatī, / the Anāvatī, the Anuṣṇā, the Sevyā, and the Kāpī, O best of men,
the Sadāvīrā, the Adhṛṣyā, and the great river Kuśacīrā, / the Rathacitrā, the Jyotirathā, the Viśvāmitrā, the Kapiñjalā,
the Candrāvahā, the Phaladā, the Kucīrā bearing water, / the Vainadī, the Piṅgalā, the Veṇā, and the great river Tuṅgavegā,
the Vidiśā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Tāmrā, and the Kapilā, / the Dhenu, the Sakāmā, the Vedasvā, the Haviḥsrāvā, the Mahāpathā,
the Śiprā, the Picchalā, and the river Bhāradvājī, / the river Kaurṇikī, the Śoṇa, the Bāhudā, and the Candramā,
the Durgā, the Antaḥśilā, the Brahmamedhyā, the Dṛṣadvatī, / the Parokṣā, the Rohī, and also the Jāmbūnadī,
the Sunāsā, the Tamasā, the Dāsī, the Sāmānyā, the Varaṇā, the Asi, / the Nīlā, the Dhṛtikarī, and the great river Parṇāśā,
the Mānavī, the Vṛṣabhā, the Bhāsā, the Brahmamedhyā, the Dṛṣadvatī— / these and many other great rivers, O best of the twice-born,
the Sadānirāmayā, the Kṛṣṇā, the Mandagā, the Mandavāhinī, / the Brāhmaṇī, the Mahāgaurī, and the Durgā, O best of men,
the Citrotpalā, the Citrarathā, the Atolā, the Rohiṇī, / the Mandākinī, the Vaitaraṇī, and the great river Kokā,
the Śuktimatī, the Anaṅgā, and the one named Vṛṣasā, / the Lauhityā, the Karatoyā, and the one named Vṛṣakā,
the Kumārī, the Ṛṣitulyā, the Māriṣā, the Sarasvatī, / the most sacred Mandākinī, and the Gaṅgā in her entirety, O best of men.
All of them are mothers of the world, and all bestow great fruit; / and there are brightly shining rivers by the hundreds and thousands.
Thus these rivers, O brāhmaṇas, have been enumerated according to tradition; / beyond this, learn from me as I speak of the countries.
There are these Kurupāñcālas, the Śālvas, the Ātreyas, the Jāṅgalas, / the Śūrasenas, the Pulindas, the Bauddhas, and likewise the Mālās,
the Matsyas, the Kuśaṭṭas, the Sauganhyas, the Kutsapas, the Kāśis, the Kośalas, / the Cedis, the Matsyas, the Karūṣas, the Bhojas, the Sindhus, the Pulindakas,
the Uttamas, the Daśārṇas, the Mekalas along with the Utkalas, / the Pāñcālas, the Kośalas, the Naikapṛṣṭhas, the Yugandharas,
the Bodhas, the Madras, the Kaliṅgas, the Kāśis, the Apara-Kāśis, / the Jaṭharas, the Kukuras, the Sudaśārṇas, O best of men,
the Kuntis, the Avantis, and likewise the Apara-Kuntis, / the Gomantas, the Mallakas, the Puṇḍras, the Vidarbhas, the Nṛpavāhikas,
the Aśmakas, the Sottaras, the younger Goparrāṣṭras, / the Adhirājyas, the Kuśaṭṭas, the Mallarāṣṭras, the Keralas,
the Mālavas, the Upavāsyas, the Cakras, the Vakrālayas, the Śakas, / the Videhas, the Magadhas, the Sadmas, the Malajas, and the Vijayas,
The Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Yakṛllomans, / the Mallas, the Sudeṣṇas, the Prahlādas, the Mahiṣas, and the Śaśakas,
the Bāhlikas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas, / the Aparāntas, the Parāntas, the Paṅkalas, and the Carmacaṇḍikas,
the Aṭavīśekharas, and the Merubhūtas, O best of men, / the Upāvṛtas, the Anupāvṛtas, the Surāṣṭras, and the Kekayas,
the Kuṭṭas, the Aparāntas, the Māheyas, the Kakṣas, those in sea retreats, / and many Andhras, O brāhmaṇas, as well as the Antargiryas,
the Bahirgiryas, the Aṅgas, the Maladas, the Magadhas, the Mālavārghaṭas, / the Sattvataras, the Prāvṛṣeyas, and the Bhārgavas, O best of the twice-born,
the Puṇḍras, the Bhārgas, the Kirātas, the Sudeṣṇas, the Bhāsuras, / the Śakas, the Niṣādas, the Niṣadhas, and the Ānartas, the Nairṛtas,
the Pūrṇalas, the Pūtimatsyas, the Kuntalas, and the Kuśakas, / the Tarigrahas, the Śūrasenas, the Ījikas, the Kalpakāraṇas,
the Tilabhāgas, the Masāras, the Madhumattas, the Kakuṃdakas, / the Kāśmīras, the Sindhu-Sauvīras, the Gāndhāras, and the Darśakas,
the Abhīsāras, the Kudrutas, the Saurilas, and the Bāhlikas, / the Darvīs, the Mālavas, the Darvas, the Vātajas, the Maras, and the Uragas.
the Balaraṭṭas, O brāhmaṇas, the Sudāmans, the Mumallikas, / the Bandhākarīkaṣas, the Kulindas, and the Gandhikas,
the Vanāyus, the Daśas, the Pārśvaromans, the Kuśabindus, / the Kacchas, the Gopālakacchas, the Jāṅgalas, the Kuruvarṇakas,
the Kirātas, the Barbaras, the Siddhas, the Vaidehas, the Tāmraliptikas, / the Auḍras, the Mlecchas, along with the Sairindhras, and the mountain-dwellers, O best of men.
Now learn of other, southern peoples, O best of sages: / the Draviḍas, the Keralas, the Prācyas, the Mūṣikas, the Bālamūṣikas,
the Karṇāṭakas, the Māhiṣakas, the Vikanthas, the Mūṣikas, / the Jhallikas, the Kuntalas, the Sauhṛdas, and the Nalakānanas.
likewise the Kaukkuṭakas, the Bolas, the Kokaṇas, the Maṇivālakas, / the Samaṅgas, the Kanakas, the Kuṅkuras, and the Aṅgāramāriṣas;
the Dhvajins, the Utsavasaṅketas, the Trivargas, the Mālyasenas, / the Vyūḍhakas, the Korakas, the Proṣṭas, and the Saṅgavegadharas;
likewise the Vindhyarulikas, the Pulindas along with the Balvalas, / the Mālavas, the Malaras, and the Aparavartakas;
the Kulidas, the Kāladas, the Caṇḍakas, the Kuraṭas, / the Muśalas, the Tanavālas, the Satīrthas, and the Pūtisṛñjayas;
the Anidāyas, the Śivāṭas, the Tapanas, the Sūtapās, / the Ṛṣikas, the Vidarbhas, the Taṅgaṇas, and the Parataṅgakas;
and the other northern barbarian peoples, O best of sages: / the Yavanas, along with the Kāmbojas, cruel barbarian tribes;
the Sakṛdgṛhas, the Kulaṭyas, the Hūṇas along with the Pārasīkas, / likewise the Ramaṇas and others, and the Daśamālikas;
and the settlements of kṣatriyas, and the families of vaiśyas and śūdras: / the Śūras, the Ābhīras, the Daradas, and the Kāśmīras along with cattle;
the Khāṇḍīkas, the Tuṣāras, the Padmagas, the Girigahvaras, / the Ādreyas, the Sabhirādājas, and likewise the Stanapoṣakas;
the Droṣakas, the Kaligas, and the tribes of the Kirātas, / the Tomaras, the Hanyamānas, and the Karabhañjakas.

These and other realms, both eastern and northern, / have been proclaimed by me, O twice-born ones, merely by designation, / as well as the great fruit of the three aims of life according to virtue and strength.

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious and great Padma Purāṇa.

3.7.m: The sages said: / O Sūta, declare to us in detail the extent of life / and the strength, whether good or bad, of this Bhārata realm and of Haimavata,
as well as the future, the past, and the present, O most virtuous one, / and likewise about Harivarṣa.
Sūta said: / In the Bhārata realm, O best of sages, there are four cosmic ages: / Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Tiṣya, O best of the twice-born.
First is the age named Kṛtayuga, then the Tretāyuga, O twice-born ones; / after that comes Dvāpara, and then Tiṣya begins.
The count of the lifespan in the Kṛta age, O best of sages, / is indeed reckoned as four thousand years, O rich in asceticism.
Likewise, they know three thousand [years] to be the lifespan in the Tretā age; / but in the Dvāpara age, two thousand [years] exist on earth at present.
There is truly no fixed lifespan in the Tiṣya age, O best of sages; / here, beings die while still in the womb, and they die just after being born.
Endowed with great strength, great vigor, and the virtue of wisdom, / they are born and have been born by the hundreds and thousands.
O twice-born, in the Kṛta age, the brāhmaṇas were strong, handsome to behold; / sages rich in austerity are born and have been born.
Full of great energy, high-souled, righteous, truthful in speech, / pleasing in appearance, handsome, possessed of great valor, archers;
Brave heroes indeed born in battle, kṣatriyas honored as warriors; / in the Tretā age, moreover, all kṣatriyas were universal monarchs.
In the Dvāpara age, all castes are constantly born / full of great energy, vigorous, yet desiring mutual destruction.
Filled with blind passion, men are wrathful indeed; / greedy and deceitful they are born in the Tiṣya age, O twice-born!
Envy, pride, wrath, deceit, and malice, / passion and greed belong to beings in the Tiṣya age, O best of men.

A decline takes place, O brāhmaṇas, in the midst of the Dvāpara age; / beyond that is the Haimavata [realm], and further still, Harivarṣa, superior in qualities.

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

3.8.m: The sages said: / The region of Jambūdvīpa has been described by you properly, O best among men; / now explain the extent of its width accurately in truth,
And the extent of the ocean, O you of faultless insight; / and speak to us of Śākadvīpa, and of righteous Kuśadvīpa,

And truly of Śālmaladvīpa, and likewise of Krauñcadvīpa. / Sūta said: / O brāhmaṇas, exceedingly numerous are the continents by which this world is filled; / I will proclaim the seven continents; listen, O foremost of the twice-born!
Eighteen thousand and six hundred full yojanas, / O best of the twice-born, is the width of Mount Jambū.
The width of the Salt Ocean is remembered to be twice that; / filled with various inhabited lands, adorned with gems and coral,
Adorned with mountains variegated with many minerals, / crowded with siddhas and cāraṇas, circular is the ocean.
And I will describe Śākadvīpa properly here, O best of men; / listen today as is fitting, O righteous ones, while I speak.
In measurement, it is twice that of Jambūdvīpa, O best of the twice-born, / in width, O fortunate ones; and the ocean likewise proportionately.
By which the ocean of milk is encircled, O tigers among sages; / holy are the lands there, and there people do not die.

Whence could there be famine, for they are endowed with forbearance and energy? / The brief summary of Śākadvīpa has been told properly, / O best of sages, O fortunate ones; what else shall I tell you?
The sages said: / The brief summary of Śākadvīpa has been told here properly, O righteous one, / by you, O very wise one; tell it in detail according to truth.
Sūta said: / Just so, O brāhmaṇas, there are seven jewel-mountains here; / there are jewel-mines and rivers; I will describe their names.
You ask about all the truth, which is exceedingly meritorious, O righteous ones! / The first is named Meru, populated by divine sages and gandharvas.
Stretching to the east, O fortunate ones, is the mountain named Malaya; / from there clouds arise and come forth on every side.
Beyond that, O sages, is the great mountain Jaladhāra; / from there Vāsava perpetually takes the excellent water.
From there rain comes forth in the rainy season, O best of the twice-born; / the lofty mountain Raivataka, where it is perpetually established.
The lunar mansion Revatī was established in heaven by the Grandfather; / to its north, O best of brāhmaṇas, is the great mountain named Śyāma.
Having the luster of a fresh cloud, lofty, glorious, with a radiant body; / from which the creatures, delighted in mind, attained a dark hue.
The sages said: / A very great doubt has arisen for us, O Sūta, from what you said: / How, O Sūta, did the creatures here fully attain a dark hue?
Sūta said: / In all these continents, O very wise ones, O foremost of sages, / there is a white and a black [color], and between those two colors, O twice-born,
A dark hue emerged; therefore it is remembered as the Śyāma mountain. / Beyond that, O best of sages, is the high mountain Durga, of great consequence;
And Keśarī, possessed of filaments, from which the wind proceeds. / The extent of those [mountains] in yojanas is doubled in respective divisions.
The realms among them, O chiefs of the twice-born, have been proclaimed by the wise: / Mahāmeru, Mahākāśa, Jalada, Kumudottara,
Jaladhāra, O highly wise one, Sukumāra, so it is remembered; / Kaumāra belongs to Raivata, and Śyāma belongs to Maṇikāñcana,
And Maudākī belongs to Keśara, and beyond is Mahānpumān. / Encompassing, O chiefs of the twice-born, both length and shortness.
it is reckoned by Jambūdvīpa; in its center is a great tree / named Śāka, O highly wise ones; its subjects are its attendants.
There the realms are sacred, and there Śaṅkara is worshipped. / The Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and deities go there.
And all the subjects are righteous, the four castes are free from envy, / engaged in their own duties, and no thief is seen there.
Long-lived, highly intelligent, free from old age and death, / the people there flourish like rivers reaching the sea in the rainy season.
The rivers there have sacred waters, and the Gaṅgā has flown [there] in many ways: / the Sukumārī, the Kumārī, the Śītā, and likewise the Śītodakā,
the Mahānadī, O brāhmaṇas, likewise the Maṇijalā river, / and the Ikṣuvardhanikā river, O best of sages, are remembered.
From there flow rivers of sacred water, exceedingly beautiful, / by hundreds of thousands, whence Indra pours rain.
It is not possible even to remember their names, / nor to count them, for those best of rivers are sacred.
Thence there are four sacred realms renowned throughout the world: / the Mṛgas, the Maśakas, and likewise the Mānasas and Mallakas.
The Mṛgas consist mostly of brāhmaṇas, twice-born men engaged in their own duties; / among the Maśakas are kṣatriyas, righteous and granting all desires.
The Mānasas are fortunate, living by the duty of vaiśyas, / endowed with all desirable things, heroic, resolute in dharma and wealth.
The Mallakas are śūdras, men always disposed to dharma. / There is no king there, O leaders of the twice-born, no punishment, and no punishers.
Knowing dharma, they protect each other solely by their own dharma. / Only this much can be spoken concerning that continent,
and only this is to be heard concerning the mighty Śākadvīpa.

3.9.m: Sūta said: / And concerning the northern continents, O brāhmaṇas, a story is heard; / listen to it, O fortunate ones, as I relate it.
The ocean of clarified butter, and another whose water is curd whey, / and the ocean of wine, and another ocean of milk;
all the continents, O bulls among the twice-born, are twice the size of one another, / and the mountains, O highly intelligent ones, are surrounded by the oceans.
Gaura is a great mountain of realgar in the middle of the continent; / the mountain in the west is Kṛṣṇa, the friend of Nārāyaṇa, O twice-born ones.
There Keśava himself protects the divine jewels, / and being pleased there, he brought about the happiness of the people.
In Śaradvīpa, a clump of kuśa grass in the middle of the realm / is worshipped, and the silk-cotton tree [is worshipped] in Śālmalidvīpa, O twice-born ones.
In Krauñcadvīpa, the great Krauñca mountain, a mine of heaps of jewels, / is constantly worshipped, O leaders of the twice-born, by the four castes.
Gomanta is an immense mountain, O brāhmaṇas, containing all minerals, / where the glorious, lotus-eyed one always resides.
Lord Nārāyaṇa Hari is always accompanied by seekers of liberation. / In Kuśadvīpa, O leaders of the twice-born, there is a mountain covered with corals:
Sunāman, very formidable; the second is the golden mountain Hemaparvata; / the third is the Kumuda mountain named Dyutimat, O leaders of the twice-born;
the fourth is named Puṣpavat, and the fifth is Kuśeśaya; / the sixth is named Harigiri; these are the six excellent mountains.
Their intermediate breadth is doubled successively according to their divisions. / The first region is Audbhida, the second is Reṇumaṇḍala,
the third is named Suratha, the fourth is remembered as Lambana, / the fifth region is Dhṛtimat, the sixth region is Prabhākara,
the seventh is the Kāpila region; these seven are the regions. / In these, gods, gandharvas, and subjects, delighted, O twice-born ones, / sport and enjoy themselves, and no person dies among them.
There are no robbers among them, nor tribes of mlecchas, O twice-born ones; / the people are mostly fair-skinned and tender, O best of men.
Concerning all the remaining ones, I will speak, O bulls among the twice-born; / listen, O twice-born ones, to what is described as it was heard, O highly intelligent ones.
In Krauñcadvīpa, O fortunate ones, is the great mountain named Krauñca; / beyond Krauñca is Vāmanaka, and beyond Vāmana is Andhakāraka.
Beyond Andhakāra, O brāhmaṇas, is the excellent mountain Maināka; / beyond Maināka, O brāhmaṇas, is the excellent mountain Govinda.
And beyond Govinda is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka; / and beyond Puṇḍarīka is proclaimed Dundubhisvana.
Their breadth ahead is double, O bulls among sages. / I shall describe the lands there; listen as I declare them.
Krauñca's land is Kuśala, Vāmana's is Manonuga; / beyond Manonuga is the land named Uṣṇa, O ascetics.
Beyond Uṣṇa is Prāvaraka, beyond Prāvara is Andhakāraka; / and beyond the Andhakāraka land, Munideśa is remembered as next.
And beyond Munideśa, Dundubhisvana is proclaimed. / It is crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas; the people are remembered as mostly fair-skinned.
These lands are declared to be inhabited by gods and gandharvas. / In Puṣkara is the mountain named Puṣkara, possessing jewels and gems.
There Lord Prajāpati himself always extends his presence; / all the gods and great ṛṣis constantly attend upon him.
With words pleasing to the mind, they worship him, O best of the twice-born. / From Jambūdvīpa proceed various jewels.
In all those continents, for the people, O best of sages, / as well as for the brāhmaṇas, by celibacy, truth, and self-restraint,
the measure of health and lifespan is doubled and doubled again. / These realms, O best of brāhmaṇas, in those continents
are declared to be realms in which a single dharma prevails. / Prajāpati, the Lord, raising his rod [of punishment], himself
constantly stands protecting these continents, O best of sages. / He is the king, he is Śiva, O brāhmaṇas, he is the father, he is the grandfather.
He protects the subjects along with the wise twice-born, O best among the twice-born. / And here, O leaders of the twice-born, food presents itself to the people;
the fortunate ones always eat it ready-prepared. / Beyond that is seen the great mountain, the support of the worlds.
It is four-cornered, O highly intelligent one, and circular on all sides. / There stand, O leaders of the twice-born, four respected by the world:
the elephants of the directions, O best of sages: Vāmana, Airāvata, Añjana, / and Supratīka, O brāhmaṇas, with faces having rut-flowing temples.
I am not able to reckon its extent here, / for it is truly immeasurable horizontally, upwards, and downwards.
There winds blow from all the directions, / and the twice-born [elephants], unbound, O best of sages, restrain them.
With lotus-like trunks of great splendor, they draw them in, / and then quickly release them again a hundredfold continually.
As the elephants of the directions breathe through mouth and nostrils, the winds / come forth, O best of the twice-born, and the subjects dwell there.
As indicated, this world together with its creation has been described by me. / Having heard this measurement of the earth, which bestows merit and pleases the mind,
the glorious man attains success, O leaders of the twice-born, esteemed by the virtuous; / his lifespan, strength, fame, and brilliance increase.
He who, observing a vow, listens to this narration on a sacred day of change, / his fathers and his grandfathers are pleased.

3.10.m:
The sages said:
Having heard from you, O fortunate one, the measure of the earth, its arrangement, and the rivers,
nectar itself has indeed been drunk.

We have heard that on that earth there are sacred tirthas.
Tell us all of them, and how they produce their fruits.
O very wise one, we wish to hear this from you in detail.

Sūta said:
O you whose wealth is asceticism, an auspicious and meritorious great narrative has been asked.
I shall tell it according to my understanding, according to propriety, and as I have heard it.

I shall recount the ancient dialogue of the divine sage Nārada
with Yudhiṣṭhira. Hear it, O best of twice-born!

Deprived of their kingdom, the sons of Pāṇḍu, those great car-warriors,
those fortunate Pāṇḍavas, dwelt in the forest together with Draupadī.

Then they saw the great-souled divine sage Nārada there,
blazing with brahmanic splendour, equal in brilliance to a blazing fire.

Surrounded by those brothers, that illustrious joy of the Kurus,
blazing with splendour, shone as does Śatakratu among the gods in heaven.

And as Sāvitrī [does not abandon] the gods, so the daughter of Yajñasena
did not abandon her husbands, the sons of Pṛthā, in accordance with dharma, as the sunlight [does not abandon] Meru.

Then, accepting their worship, the venerable sage Nārada
consoled the son of Dharma with suitable and affectionate [words].

And he spoke to the great-souled Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira:
“Speak, O best of upholders of dharma! What is to be requested? I shall indeed give it to you.”

Then the king, the son of Dharma, bowing together with his brothers,
spoke these words with folded hands to Nārada, who was equal to a god:

“When you are pleased, O fortunate one, revered by all the worlds,
I consider everything accomplished, O you of noble vows, by your grace.

Yet if I, together with my brothers, am worthy of your favour, O sinless one,
you ought to cut down the doubt residing in my heart, O best of sages.

He who, devoted to sacred tirthas, circumambulates the earth—
what is the fruit of that in full? You ought to tell that, O holy one!”

Nārada said:
Hear, O king, attentively, how of old Dilīpa
heard all this in the presence of Vasiṣṭha.

Of old, on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, Dilīpa, best of kings,
undertaking a righteous vow, was dwelling then like a sage

in an auspicious, meritorious region worshipped by divine sages, O great king,
at Gaṅgādvāra, frequented by gods and gandharvas, he of great splendour.

He of supreme splendour offered oblations to the ancestors and to the gods,
and he offered oblations to the sages according to the rites prescribed by rule.

Then, at some time, as that noble-minded one was reciting prayers,
he saw the highest sage Vasiṣṭha, resembling a divine being.

Seeing his royal chaplain blazing, as it were, with splendour,
he gained incomparable joy and was filled with supreme wonder.

He worshipped him who had arrived, O great king, O Bhārata,
for he, the best among upholders of dharma, [did so] through rites prescribed by rule.

Taking water for the guest-offering upon his head, pure, with concentrated mind,
he proclaimed his name before that best of brahmin sages.

“I am Dilīpa, may you have good fortune; I am your servant, O you of noble vows!
By the very sight of you I am freed from all sins.”

Having spoken thus, O great king, Dilīpa, best of men,
controlling his speech, with folded hands, remained silent, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

Seeing Dilīpa, that best of kings, emaciated
by restraint and by study of the sacred texts, the sage became pleased at heart.

3.11.m:
Vasiṣṭha said:
By this modesty of yours, O knower of dharma, by your self-control,
and by your truthfulness, O fortunate one, I am pleased with you in every way.

Since you possess such dharma, your ancestors have been delivered by you;
therefore you see me, O son, and you are my sacrificer, O sinless one.

My delight in you grows today; speak, what shall I do for you?
Whatever you say, O best of men, I shall grant it to you, O sinless one.

Dilīpa said:
O knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, revered by all the worlds,
I consider everything accomplished indeed, since I have seen the master.

Yet if I am worthy of your favour, O best of upholders of dharma,
I shall ask a doubt residing in my heart; you ought to tell it to me.

I have a certain doubt regarding the dharma of tirthas, O lord;
therefore I wish to hear an account of them from you one by one.

He who circumambulates the earth, O best of twice-born—
what is his fruit, O brahmin sage? Tell me that, O you whose wealth is asceticism!

Vasiṣṭha said:
I shall narrate that which is the resolve of the sages, committed to me.
Listen, therefore, with one-pointed mind, dear one, to the fruit that exists regarding tirthas.

He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who has knowledge, austerity, and renown, enjoys the fruit of tirthas.

He who turns away from accepting gifts, is content, restrained, pure,
and free from egotism, enjoys the fruit of tirthas.

He who is free from deceit, eats nothing, eats only what is obtained without asking, has his senses conquered,
and is released from all defects, enjoys the fruit of tirthas.

He who is free from anger, O king of kings, whose nature is truth, whose vows are firm,
and who regards all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of tirthas.

Sacrifices have been proclaimed by the sages among the gods in due order,
as well as their fruit in truth, in the hereafter and here in every way.

Those sacrifices cannot be obtained by a poor person, O ruler of the earth;
sacrifices require many implements and have an extensive array of various provisions.

These are obtained by kings or by wealthy men in some places,
not by crowds of poor men, solitary and lacking resources.

Learn that rite, O ruler of men, which can be accomplished even by the poor,
equal in holy fruits to sacrifices, O ruler of the earth!

This supreme secret of the sages, O best of upholders of dharma—
the holy pilgrimage to tirthas—is superior even to sacrifices.

Without fasting for three nights and without visiting tirthas,
and without giving gold and cows, one truly becomes poor.

Having sacrificed with sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with lavish priestly gifts,
one does not attain that fruit which is gained by visiting tirthas.

In the world of mortals is the tirtha of the world of gods, renowned in the three worlds;
having reached the tirtha Puṣkara, one becomes equal to the god of gods.

There are ten thousand crores of tirthas, O ruler of the earth,
whose presence is at Puṣkara at the three junctures of the day, O descendant of the solar line.

The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Sādhyas along with the troops of Maruts,
as well as the gandharvas and apsarases, are present there, O lord.

Where the gods, having performed austerities, as well as the Daityas and brahmin sages,
the twice-born possessed of divine yoga, [attained their ends] through great merit, O great king—

of the wise one who desires Puṣkara even with the mind,
all sins are purified, and he is honoured in the vault of heaven.

In this tirtha, O fortunate one, the Grandfather constantly
dwelt, supremely pleased, honoured by gods and dānavas.

At Puṣkara, O fortunate one, the gods, preceded by the sages,
attained supreme perfection, endowed with great merit.

Whoever performs a bath there, devoted to worshipping the ancestors and the gods—
the wise proclaim it to be ten times [the fruit] of a horse sacrifice.

If one should feed even a single brahmin while resorting to the forest of Puṣkara,
by that he goes to the honoured worlds residing in the abode of Brahmā.
Whoever remembers Puṣkara evening and morning with joined palms / has performed ritual bathing in all sacred sites, O king.
Whatever sin has been committed from birth by a woman or a man / is completely destroyed the moment one reaches Puṣkara.
Just as Madhusūdana is the foremost of all gods, / even so Puṣkara, O king, is declared to be the foremost of sacred sites.
Having dwelt for twelve years at Puṣkara, restrained and pure, / one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
One who maintains the agnihotra fire for a full hundred years, / or dwells for one Kārttika full moon at Puṣkara—the two are entirely equal.
It is difficult to go to Puṣkara; difficult is austerity at Puṣkara; / difficult is giving gifts at Puṣkara; and very difficult indeed it is to dwell there.
Three white peaks and three cascades: / these are the Puṣkara sacred sites, the primal shrines; we do not know the reason for that.
Having dwelt there for twelve years, self-controlled and regulated in diet, / one is freed from all sins and obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.

3.12.m: Vasiṣṭha said: / Having completed the circumambulation, one should enter Jambūmārga; / having entered Jambūmārga, which is honored by the ancestors, gods, and sages,
One obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / Having dwelt there for five nights, eating only at the sixth mealtime, a man
Does not attain an evil state of existence, and attains unsurpassed perfection. / Having returned from Jambūmārga, one should proceed to the hermitage of Taṇḍulika;
One does not attain an evil state of existence, and is honored in the heavenly world. / Having reached the hermitage of Agastya, intent upon worshipping the ancestors and gods,
Fasting for three nights, O king, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. / Subsisting on vegetables or on fruits, one attains the supreme state of youth.
Having reached Kanyāśrama, thriving with auspicious splendor and honored by the world— / for that is the holy and primordial Dharmāraṇya, O best of kings—
Where, immediately upon entering, one is completely freed from sins; / having worshipped the ancestors and gods, disciplined and regulated in diet,
One enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires. / Then, having circumambulated, one should proceed to Yayātipatana;
There indeed one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / From there, self-controlled and regulated in diet, one should go to Mahākāla.
Bathing at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / Then one knowing dharma should go to the holy place, the tirtha of Umā's husband,
renowned in the three worlds by the name of Bhadravaṭa. / Approaching Īśāna there, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows,
and by Mahādeva's grace he attains the status of Gaṇapati, / prosperous, without rivals, and endowed with fortune, O best of men.
Reaching the Narmadā, the river famous throughout the three worlds, / and offering libations to the ancestors and gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

3.13.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / An excellent tirtha was described by Vasiṣṭha to Dilīpa, / renowned as the Narmadā, shattering the mountain of sins.
I wish to hear more; tell me that, O Nārada: / the glorification of the Narmadā spoken by Vasiṣṭha, O best of the twice-born.
How is this greatly meritorious river famous everywhere, / celebrated by the name Narmadā? Tell me that, O Nārada.
Nārada said: / The Narmadā is the best of rivers, destroying all sins; / she redeems all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
The glorification of the Narmadā as spoken by Vasiṣṭha was heard by me; / I shall relate all of it to you, O great king.
The Gaṅgā is holy at Kanakhala, the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra; / but whether in a village or in a forest, the Narmadā is holy everywhere.
The water of the Sarasvatī purifies in three days, and that of the Yamunā in seven days; / the Gaṅgā's water purifies immediately, while the Narmadā's [purifies] by merely seeing it.
In the country of Kaliṅga, in its western half, on Mount Amarakṇṭaka, / she is sacred in the three worlds, delightful, and charming.
Together with the gods, Asuras, and Gandharvas, the ṛṣis rich in asceticism, / having performed austerities there, O great king, have attained supreme perfection.
Bathing there, O great king, remaining steadfast in observances, with senses subdued, / and fasting for a single night, one redeems a hundred ancestral lines.
A man who bathes at Janeśvara and offers a rice ball according to the rules— / his ancestors are satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
All around the mountain, Rudrakoṭi is established. / Whoever bathes there, offering perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
the entire Rudrakoṭi will be pleased with him, of this there is no doubt. / On the western side of the mountain dwells Lord Maheśvara himself.
Bathing there, being purified, celibate, with senses subdued, / one should perform the ancestral rites according to the prescribed rules.
There alone one should satisfy the ancestral deities with water and sesame seeds; / his family up to the seventh generation remains in heaven, O Pāṇḍava.
For sixty thousand years he is glorified in the heavenly realm, / thronged by multitudes of apsarases, surrounded by divine women,
anointed with divine perfumes, and adorned with celestial ornaments. / Then, falling from heaven, he is born in a large family;
he is born wealthy, charitable, and righteous; / he remembers that tirtha again and journeys there.
Having redeemed a hundred lineages, he goes to the realm of Rudra. / That best of rivers is heard to be more than a hundred yojanas [long],
and its width, O king of kings, is an interval of two yojanas. / Sixty thousand tirthas, and likewise sixty crores,
are situated all around the mountain at Amarakṇṭaka. / Becoming celibate, purified, having conquered anger and subdued the senses,
desisting from all violence, and rejoicing in the welfare of all beings, / observing all such proper conduct, one should circumambulate the guardians of the sacred place.
Listen attentively to me concerning his meritorious reward, O king: / For a hundred thousand years he rejoices in heaven, O Pāṇḍava,
thronged by multitudes of apsarases, attended by divine women, / anointed with divine perfumes, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
He disports himself in the world of the gods and rejoices with the deities. / Then, falling from heaven, he becomes a mighty king.
He obtains a palace adorned with various jewels, / with divine jewel-encrusted pillars adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,
filled with divine paintings and accompanied by female and male servants; / and by the sounds of rutting elephants and the neighing of horses,
his gate is bustling like the abode of Indra. / He becomes an overlord of kings, glorious, beloved of all women.
Dwelling in that palace, endowed with pleasures and sports, / he lives for a full hundred years, free from all diseases.
Such enjoyment belongs to him who dies at Amarakṇṭaka, / through entering fire, or in water, and likewise through fasting.
His destination is one from which there is no return, as into the sky from the mountain. / That man who falls from the precipice, O lord of men,
three thousand maidens for each, and others as well, / stand in his palace and plead to be sent on errands.
Provided with divine pleasures, he plays for an inexhaustible time. / On earth, as far as the ocean, no such man is born
as this one [who dies], O best of men, on Mount Amarakṇṭaka. / Koṭitīrtha is to be known on the western side of the mountain,
where Rudra is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Jāleśvara. / By offering a rice ball there, and by the rite of twilight devotion,
one's ancestors are satisfied for ten years. / To the south of the Narmadā is the great river named Kapilā,
covered with sarala and arjuna trees, situated not very far away; / she is meritorious, exceedingly blessed, and renowned in the three worlds.
There are more than a hundred crores of tirthas there, O Yudhiṣṭhira; / it is heard in the Purāṇa, O king, that everything becomes a crore times greater.
The trees on its bank that fall in the course of time, / coming into contact with the waters of the Narmadā, also go to the supreme state.
The second [river] is the exceedingly blessed, auspicious Viśalyakaraṇā; / a man bathing on its bank becomes free from pain in an instant.
All the hosts of gods, together with Kinnaras and great serpents, / Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and ṛṣis rich in asceticism,
all assembled there on Mount Amarakṇṭaka. / And having assembled, all those sages rich in asceticism
brought forth the holy [stream] adhering to the Narmadā, named Viśalyā by name, / highly blessed and destroying all sins.
A man bathing there, O king, celibate, with senses subdued, / fasting for a single night, redeems a hundred ancestral lines.
The Kapilā and the Viśalyā, it is heard, O best of kings, / were proclaimed in the Purāṇa by the Lord out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Bathing there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice; / and whoever undertakes fasting at that tirtha, O lord of men,
with a soul completely purified of all sins, he goes to the realm of Indra. / As for what was heard by me in the Purāṇa regarding the Narmadā, O king of kings,
bathing here and there [along it], a man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / Those who dwell on its northern bank dwell in the realm of Indra.
At the Sarasvatī, at the Gaṅgā, and at the Narmadā, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / giving gifts and bathing are equal, just as Śaṅkara told me.
He who gives up his life on Mount Amarakṇṭaka / is honored in the realm of Indra for more than a hundred crores of years.
The holy water of the Narmadā, adorned with waves of foam, / is pure, to be saluted with the head; one is freed from all sins.
The Narmadā is all-meritorious and removes the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa; / by fasting for a day and night [by it], one is freed from the killing of a brāhmaṇa.
Thus holy and delightful is the Narmadā, O son of Pāṇḍu; / this great river purifies even the three worlds.

At Vaṭeśvara, greatly meritorious, at Gaṅgādvāra, and in penance-groves— / for those of strict vows who have practiced austerities in all these places, / ten times more merit is heard to be gained at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Udvasā.

3.14.m: Nārada said: / The Narmadā is indeed the best of rivers, holy, and the holiest in the three [worlds]; / it was divided by the fortunate sages who desired dharma.
It was partitioned [into sacred stretches] only a sacrificial thread's measure apart, O Pāṇḍava; / having bathed in them, O king of kings, one is freed from all sins.
And as to the sacred bathing-place Jaleśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds, / listen, O son of Pāṇḍu, as I tell of its origin.
Formerly, all the assemblies of sages, together with Indra and the hosts of Maruts, / praised the great-souled Maheśvara, the god of gods.
Singing praise, they arrived where Lord Maheśvara was; / together with Indra, the hosts of Maruts made petition to the lord of gods: / 'O three-eyed lord, protect us who are agitated by fear, O Lord!
The Lord said: / Welcome, O best of sages! For what purpose have you come here? / What is the grief, what the anguish, or whence has fear arisen?
Tell me, O fortunate ones; I wish to know this.' / Thus spoken to by Rudra, those of unmeasured vows spoke:
The ṛṣis said: / There is indeed a terrible dānava of great valor, arrogant with strength, / renowned by the name Bāṇa, whose city is Tripura.
Dwelling in the sky, that celestial [city] revolves by his splendor; / frightened by him, O three-eyed one, we have taken refuge in you alone.
Protect us from this great misery, O god; for you are the supreme refuge; / thus, O lord of gods, you ought to show grace to all,
so that the gods may become well-pleased, increase in happiness, O Śaṅkara, / and attain supreme contentment; you ought to do that, O Lord.'
The God said: / 'I shall do all this; do not be despondent; / in no long time at all, I shall bring about what brings you joy.'
Having comforted them all and stationed himself on the bank of the Narmadā, / the lord of all reflected upon his slaying, O Pāṇḍava:
'How and by what means is Tripura to be slain by me?' / Having thus reflected, the Blessed One then remembered Nārada; / simply by being remembered, Nārada arrived and was present.
Nārada said: / 'Command me, O Mahādeva! Why indeed have I been summoned? / What is the deed to be done by me, O god? Tell me.'
The Lord said: / 'Go, Nārada, to that very place where that city Tripura is, / belonging to Bāṇa, the chief of dānavas; go quickly and do this:
The husbands possess the radiance of deities, and the women resemble apsarases; / by their splendor alone, O brāhmaṇa, does Tripura revolve in the sky.
Going there, O chief of brāhmaṇas, urge upon them another counsel.' / Hearing the word of the god, the sage, swift of step,
entered that city to corrupt the hearts of the women; / that celestial city shone, adorned with various jewels,
a hundred yojanas wide, and twice as long as that; / then he saw right there Bāṇa, arrogant with strength,
resplendent with garlands, earrings, armlets, and a diadem, / covered with pearl necklaces and gems, and adorned with the luster of the moon.
His women were rich with gems; the men were adorned with gold; / seeing Nārada, the mighty chief of the dānavas arose.
Bāṇa said: / 'That divine sage himself has now come to my home; / let water for respect and foot-water be offered according to custom, O best of the twice-born!
After a long time, the brāhmaṇa has arrived; please sit upon this seat.' / Having thus honored Nārada who was present,
his wife, the queen named Anaupamyā, [spoke to him].
Anaupamyā said: / 'O venerable one, by what are the gods pleased in the mortal world— / by a vow, by an observance, or by gift-giving, or by austerity?'
Nārada said: / 'Whoever gives a cow made of sesame to a brāhmaṇa versed in the Vedas / has given the earth with its oceans and nine continents.
In aerial cars resembling ten million suns and fulfilling all desires, / he rejoices for an imperishable time, his command long established.
Hog-plums, wood-apples, and a grove of plantains, / kadambas, campakas, aśokas, and various manifold trees—
and the eighth, the fourth, and both the twelfth [tithis], / the solar transit, the equinox, and the opening of an intercalary period—
all these are holy; those women who fast [on these], / endowed with dharma, their residence is in heaven, no doubt.
Freed from the age of Kali and rid of all sins, / women intent on fasting are not approached by ascetics.'
Having heard this, O woman of beautiful hips, you ought to do as you please.' / Having heard Nārada's words, the queen spoke these words:
'Grant your favor, O chief of brāhmaṇas; accept a gift as you desire— / gold, jewels, gems, garments, and ornaments.
I shall give that to you, O brāhmaṇa, and whatever else is hard to obtain; / accept it, O best of the twice-born, so that Hari and Śaṅkara may be pleased.'
Nārada said: / 'Let it be given to someone else, O good lady—to a brāhmaṇa whose livelihood is diminished; / we are rich in good character, and devotion is practiced by me.'
Having thus stolen their minds and instructed them all, / he went, O best of the Bharatas, back to his own abode.
Their minds being captivated here, their thoughts were directed elsewhere; / a flaw arose in the city of the great-souled Bāṇa.
